summary: This experimental memo gives instructions for IANA allocations needed by the Seamoby protocols, CARD and CXTP, which are designed to speed up handovers between wireless access routers. It covers the code points those protocols need, such as ICMP and SCTP values.

eli5.summary: Two new mobility protocols need official numbers so they do not clash with others. This document says which numbers to hand out.

questions: what code points do card and cxtp need
subtitle: Reserve network numbers for experimental wireless handover protocols.

tldr.problem: Two experimental protocols, CARD and CXTP, were designed to speed up IP handovers between wireless access routers, but they need official numbers for ICMP types, SCTP ports and other protocol identifiers to avoid clashing with other protocols.
tldr.mechanism: This memo instructs IANA to allocate specific code points and establish registries for the Seamoby protocols to use. It also defines a shared ICMP extension format that other experimental mobility protocols can reuse.
tldr.outcome: The protocols got their allocations, and the extensible ICMP format became available for future experimental mobility work, though the Seamoby protocols themselves never saw widespread deployment.

today: RFC 4065 is an Experimental protocol that has not been obsoleted or superseded. The Seamoby protocols themselves did not achieve widespread deployment, but the extensible ICMP format remains available for future experimental mobility protocols to use.

sections.title: The Need for Protocol Numbers
sections.content:
Two experimental protocols designed to accelerate IP handover between wireless access routers required official numbers from IANA to avoid colliding with other protocols. These were the Candidate Access Router Discovery (CARD) protocol and the Context Transfer Protocol (CXTP), both described in related RFCs.

Because these protocols were experimental with no guarantee of widespread adoption, the RFC takes a conservative approach to numbering. The ICMP extension format it defines was also designed to be reusable by other experimental mobility protocols in the future.
sections.eli5: When you make up a new protocol, you need a number so messages do not get mixed up with others. This RFC says what numbers to hand out.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Code Points
sections.content:
IANA assigned SCTP port numbers 5090 and 5091 for CARD and CXTP to use. For IPv4, ICMP type 41 was assigned for experimental mobility messages. For IPv6, ICMP type code 150 was assigned for the same purpose.

Mobile IPv4 Foreign Agent Discovery option codes were also allocated: code 137 for CARD MN-AR signatures, code 138 for CARD requests and code 139 for CARD replies. For IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, codes 138 and 139 were allocated for CARD request and reply options.
sections.eli5: Think of these as addresses and mailbox numbers in the protocol world. Each protocol gets its own number so the post office knows where to deliver it.

sections.title: Registries for Message Options
sections.content:
CARD required two new registries: one for Attribute-Value Pairs (AVP) type codes and one for Layer 2 Access Technology identifiers. The AVP Type Registry allows future expansion of the CARD protocol message space. The Layer 2 Access Technology Identifier Registry maps type codes to specific technologies like Ethernet, IEEE 802.11 variants, Bluetooth and IEEE 802.16.

CXTP required a Context Transfer Profile Type Registry for identifying types of feature contexts that can be carried in CXTP messages. The first profile type registered was IPv6 Multicast Listener Context.
sections.eli5: These are like filing cabinets where people can add new categories without breaking what was already there.

sections.title: Shared Format for Future Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC defines an ICMP Experimental Mobility Type with a subtype field that identifies the specific protocol. For IPv4 this is ICMP type 41; for IPv6 it is ICMP type code 150. Within this message, a one-octet subtype field identifies whether the message is for CARD (subtype 0) or CXTP (subtype 1).

This design allows other experimental mobility protocols to reuse the same ICMP type without collision, merely by using a different subtype code. Subsequent allocations of subtype codes are made by the Specification Required method, conserving numbering resources.
sections.eli5: Instead of giving each new mobility game its own mailbox, they all share one mailbox but put a label inside saying whose turn it is.
